hints: Focus on what changes when $\text{NH}_3$ becomes $\text{NH}_4^+$, think about the lone pair on nitrogen.
Count the bonding pairs and lone pairs around N in $\text{NH}_4^+$, you should find 4 bonding pairs and 0 lone pairs.
Recall the shape and ideal angle for 4 bonding pairs with no lone pairs, and compare it to the pyramidal $107^\circ$ of ammonia.
walkthrough:
**Recall the shape of ammonia**

Ammonia, $\text{NH}_3$, has 3 bonding pairs and 1 lone pair on nitrogen. That gives a pyramidal shape with angle about $107^\circ$.

$$\text{NH}_3: 3 \text{ bond pairs} + 1 \text{ lone pair} \rightarrow \text{pyramidal, } 107^\circ$$

**See what the $\text{H}^+$ does**

The $\text{H}^+$ has no electrons, so it accepts the lone pair from $\text{NH}_3$ to form a dative covalent bond. The lone pair is now used up.

$$\text{NH}_3 + \text{H}^+ \rightleftharpoons \text{NH}_4^+$$

**Apply VSEPR to $\text{NH}_4^+$**

In $\text{NH}_4^+$, nitrogen now has 4 bonding pairs and 0 lone pairs. Four pairs spread out equally to minimise repulsion.

$$4 \text{ bond pairs} + 0 \text{ lone pairs} \rightarrow \text{tetrahedral, } 109.5^\circ$$

options.A: This describes ammonia, $\text{NH}_3$, not the ammonium ion. Students often pick this by forgetting that the lone pair is lost when the fourth N-H bond forms.
options.B: Pyramidal shape always goes with about $107^\circ$ because of the lone pair. This row mixes the old shape with the new angle, so it is inconsistent.
options.C: The shape is correct, but $107^\circ$ is the pyramidal angle when a lone pair is present. Once there are 4 equal bonding pairs and no lone pair, the angle opens up to $109.5^\circ$.
options.D: With 4 bonding pairs and no lone pairs, $\text{NH}_4^+$ is tetrahedral with the perfect tetrahedral angle of $109.5^\circ$. This is the correct VSEPR prediction.
